title: Episode 39: Accessibility Agents - Complete Reference
description: All 55 agents, all 54+ slash commands, customization, and troubleshooting.
concepts: Complete documentation for the 55 agents across 3 teams (Accessibility, GitHub Workflow, Developer Tools)
All 54+ slash commands with detailed usage examples
Customization: agent instruction files and settings
Troubleshooting: agent not responding, wrong output, context issues
Building on the agent system for custom domain-specific agents
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. This time we’re building a practical mental map for accessibility agents and the wider customization system around them. Think of this as a reference episode in conversation form: not just what the files are called, but when you’d use each one, how they interact, where they live, and how to keep the workflow accessible.

[JAMIE]
So this is the episode for the learner who keeps seeing things like .agent.md, .prompt.md, SKILL.md, copilot-instructions.md, and maybe hooks JSON, and is thinking, I know these are related, but I do not yet have the whole picture.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And one important update right at the start: older GitHub materials about building Copilot Extensions now point toward MCP documentation. The GitHub App based extension model has effectively been superseded by MCP servers as the standard extensibility path. But custom .agent.md files are still a primary way to define agent personas and behavior in editor-based workflows.

[JAMIE]
That helps. So learners should understand both the newer MCP direction and the continuing importance of file-based agent customization.

[ALEX]
Yes. Also, this appendix is a companion reference to the earlier lesson on accessibility agents and the chapter about building your own agent. So here we’re doing the full map.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
At the highest level, the ecosystem described here includes 80 agents across three teams, available across five platforms, along with more than 54 slash commands, more than 25 reusable skills, and several instruction file types.

[JAMIE]
That’s a lot. If I’m blind or low vision and trying to keep this organized mentally, what’s the cleanest first split?

[ALEX]
Start with four buckets. First, agents: named helpers you can invoke, often with an at-sign. Second, prompts or slash commands: reusable commands that package a task. Third, instructions: always-on or file-targeted guidance that shapes model behavior. Fourth, supporting automation and preferences, like hooks and personal settings.

[JAMIE]
And the platforms matter too, right?

[ALEX]
They do. In this reference, the platforms are GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, and Codex CLI. VS Code with GitHub Copilot is the central daily-workflow environment, especially because it combines agent files, tools, inline suggestions, and accessible editor navigation. Other platforms use different installation or configuration patterns, but many of the ideas transfer.

[JAMIE]
Can we walk through those platforms in plain language?

[ALEX]
Sure. GitHub Copilot in VS Code uses .github/agents with .agent.md files and is best for everyday editor work. Claude Code emphasizes autonomous multi-file work with terminal and file management. Gemini CLI is command-line oriented and can integrate search workflows. Claude Desktop is more session-oriented, with persistent context and longer-running interaction. Codex CLI is described here as experimental and uses its own configuration style.

[JAMIE]
So same broad idea, different homes and capabilities.

[ALEX]
Right.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now the three agent teams. Team one is Accessibility, with 40 agents. Team two is GitHub Workflow, with 20 agents. Team three is Developer Tools, with 18 agents.

[JAMIE]
Let’s start with the accessibility team, because that’s probably the emotional center of this lesson.

[ALEX]
Agreed. The accessibility team covers web and document accessibility across the WCAG spectrum, from basic conformance work through more advanced and sometimes AAA-oriented guidance. The key point is specialization. You have orchestrators, task agents, and informational agents.

[JAMIE]
What’s the difference?

[ALEX]
An orchestrator coordinates. A task agent performs a specialized kind of analysis or output. An informational agent explains standards, testing approaches, or background material.

[JAMIE]
Give me some anchor examples.

[ALEX]
@accessibility-lead is an orchestrator that can delegate across specialist agents. @web-accessibility-wizard is another orchestrator, but guided, with severity scoring, remediation tracking, and action plans. On the task side, @aria-specialist focuses on ARIA roles, states, properties, and widget patterns. @modal-specialist handles dialogs, focus trapping, escape behavior, and announcement concerns. @keyboard-navigator looks at tab order, focus management, shortcuts, skip links, and traps. @forms-specialist covers labels, validation, error handling, autocomplete, and grouping.

[JAMIE]
And for content structure?

[ALEX]
That’s where agents like @alt-text-headings and @markdown-a11y-assistant become useful. They focus on alt text quality, heading hierarchy, landmarks, tables, link clarity, emoji use, and document structure. Then you have @tables-specialist, @link-checker, and @live-region-controller for narrower domains.

[JAMIE]
I also noticed broader or more specialized areas.

[ALEX]
Yes. There are agents for cognitive accessibility, mobile accessibility, email, media, data visualizations, web components, performance impacts on accessibility, internationalization and right-to-left language support, compliance mapping, accessibility statements, and design system auditing.

[JAMIE]
And documents are their own cluster.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, ePub, cross-document analysis, document inventories, CSV reporting, and a document accessibility wizard. That matters because accessibility work is not just websites. Many teams need accessible office documents and PDFs, and these agents reflect that.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now what about the GitHub workflow team?

[ALEX]
These 20 agents support repository operations: issues, pull requests, analytics, CI, releases, notifications, repository administration, and related collaboration tasks. The quick-reference section especially highlights a few agents that are central for day-to-day work.

[JAMIE]
Let’s do those carefully.

[ALEX]
First, @daily-briefing. This is a morning situation report for issues, PRs, CI status, security, and community activity. The accessibility-specific note is that its output uses H2 headings so screen reader users can navigate quickly with heading shortcuts, like pressing H in many reading modes.

[JAMIE]
That’s an important design pattern: an agent is not just smart, it formats its output for navigation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Accessibility is as much about structure as content.

[JAMIE]
What’s next?

[ALEX]
@issue-tracker for issue management across repositories: finding, prioritizing, triaging, and drafting replies. Then @pr-review for structured pull request review with risk assessment, change maps, and suggestions. Its output is called out as using H2 and H3 headings, again to support heading-based navigation.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m listening with a screen reader or reading in an accessible view, I can jump section by section rather than wading through a wall of text.

[ALEX]
Precisely. Then @analytics gives team-level insight like contribution velocity, turnaround time, code hotspots, and workload distribution. @insiders-a11y-tracker monitors accessibility-sensitive changes, including WCAG and ARIA related shifts, headings, links, and keyboard-related regressions.

[JAMIE]
What exactly does that tracker monitor?

[ALEX]
In spirit, anything likely to affect accessibility in a meaningful way: semantic structure changes, link text shifts, heading hierarchy changes, keyboard interactions, ARIA updates, and similar high-risk changes. Finally, @template-builder is an interactive wizard for issue templates through ask-and-answer interaction.

[JAMIE]
That sounds helpful for learners who don’t want to memorize YAML structure.

[ALEX]
Very much so.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The reference also points to supporting resources and reusable skills. Skills are packaged know-how that can be loaded when relevant, rather than always being fully active.

[JAMIE]
And there are also learning cards.

[ALEX]
Right. Several sections include learning-card style summaries, meant to reinforce the core mental model: how the ecosystem fits together, how invocation works, how skills differ from agents, and which features are cross-platform.

[JAMIE]
So the appendix is trying to be both a technical reference and a study tool.

[ALEX]
Yes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now I want the file and scope story, because that’s where people get confused. What applies always? What applies only to some files? What wins in conflicts?

[ALEX]
Great question. The appendix describes scope and priority across multiple levels. The three main scopes are user level, workspace level, and more specific file or folder targeting.

[JAMIE]
User level means personal and cross-workspace?

[ALEX]
Exactly. User-level files are your own preferences and instructions that follow you across projects. Workspace-level files are repository-shared and meant for the whole team. Then there are targeted files, like .instructions.md with applyTo patterns, which narrow behavior to particular file types or paths.

[JAMIE]
And priority?

[ALEX]
Highest priority wins when there’s conflict, and the more specific scope generally overrides the broader one. So a targeted instruction for Markdown files can override general always-on guidance, and repository guidance can override your general expectations where the tool honors that precedence model.

[JAMIE]
What about combining multiple files?

[ALEX]
Multiple files can be merged. The general idea is additive combination when instructions don’t conflict, and priority-based resolution when they do. That’s why being explicit and non-duplicative matters.

[JAMIE]
Can you ground that in locations?

[ALEX]
At user level, think personal, cross-workspace locations. At workspace level, think repo-shared locations inside the project, especially under .github or dedicated customization folders depending on the file type and platform. The appendix emphasizes both categories because discoverability depends heavily on correct placement.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
That brings us to always-on instructions. The recommended option is .github/copilot-instructions.md.

[JAMIE]
Why is that the recommended default?

[ALEX]
Because it’s simple, repository-shared, and intended as an always-on instruction layer for the project. If your team wants the assistant to consistently follow accessibility standards, documentation style rules, commit message conventions, and tone guidelines, this is a strong home for that.

[JAMIE]
And this appendix even includes a sample set of copilot instructions for accessibility-agents, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. The sample covers accessibility standards, documentation style, commit message format, and tone. That means you can tell the assistant, in effect: use semantic headings, write accessible Markdown, keep explanations structured, use a chosen commit message convention, and adopt an appropriate review voice.

[JAMIE]
So this is where teams define their baseline values.

[ALEX]
Well put.

[JAMIE]
What are the other options?

[ALEX]
Option B is AGENTS.md, useful for multi-tool or monorepo contexts. A root-level AGENTS.md can apply broadly, and nested AGENTS.md files may apply per subfolder, though the appendix notes that nested behavior is experimental. Option C is CLAUDE.md for Claude Code compatibility. Option D is settings-based instructions, but those are marked deprecated. There are also organization-level instructions for GitHub Enterprise.

[JAMIE]
And there’s a note about enabling discovery in VS Code?

[ALEX]
Yes. Some org-level or shared setups require making sure VS Code can discover those instructions. In practice, that means paying attention to supported locations and product documentation so the editor actually loads what you expect.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay. Always-on instructions are the baseline. What if I want instructions only for certain file types?

[ALEX]
Then you move to .instructions.md files. These are file-based instructions with targeting support.

[JAMIE]
What do learners need to know first?

[ALEX]
Three things: location, frontmatter, and applyTo. File locations determine whether the file is discovered. Frontmatter carries metadata. And applyTo is the glob pattern that says which files the instructions should affect.

[JAMIE]
Let’s slow down on applyTo.

[ALEX]
applyTo is how you say, for example, “use these rules for all Markdown files,” or “only for issue template YAML files,” or “only for docs under a certain folder.” It uses glob-style matching. So the power here is precision.

[JAMIE]
And discovery modes?

[ALEX]
That’s about how the environment finds and activates instruction files. Depending on tooling, files may be discovered automatically from expected locations or surfaced through creation workflows in the editor.

[JAMIE]
The appendix gives examples too.

[ALEX]
Yes. One example is accessibility-specific instructions for Markdown accessibility standards. Another is YAML issue template instructions, specifically for issue template YAML standards. Those examples show how you can keep guidance close to the artifact type.

[JAMIE]
That seems especially good for accessibility. Instead of vague “be accessible” guidance, you can say exactly how Markdown should be structured, or exactly how issue forms should be written.

[ALEX]
Exactly. This reduces drift and improves consistency.

[JAMIE]
And there are practical creation methods.

[ALEX]
Two are called out: a Command Palette method and a quick creation method. The appendix also repeats the “creating an instructions file” topic, underscoring that this is a common task. Learners should know both routes: using the editor’s guided command flow, or just creating the file directly in the proper location with the proper frontmatter.

[JAMIE]
What about writing effective instructions?

[ALEX]
Keep them specific, testable, and scoped. Avoid contradictory guidance. Prefer concrete requirements over aspirational language. And make accessibility requirements explicit, not implied.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now for the star of the show: .agent.md.

[ALEX]
Yes. A .agent.md file defines a custom agent. The appendix treats this as a complete format reference.

[JAMIE]
What are the big pieces?

[ALEX]
File locations, frontmatter, model fallback, invocation control, allowed tools, body structure, constraints, behavior, output format, section headers, accessibility requirements, scope boundaries, and how to create your own agent.

[JAMIE]
Start with frontmatter.

[ALEX]
Frontmatter is the metadata block at the top. It identifies the agent and controls things like model choices, tool access, invocation behavior, and related properties. One especially useful idea is model fallback arrays: if a preferred model is unavailable, the system can try alternates in a specified order.

[JAMIE]
That’s a reliability feature.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then there’s invocation control, which governs how the agent is called or surfaced. Some agents are meant to be directly invoked with an at-sign. Others may be chosen by workflows or commands.

[JAMIE]
The tool list sounded important too.

[ALEX]
Very. The appendix describes all tool names, built-in aliases, exact-name references, and recommended tool combinations by use case. This matters because tools define the agent’s power and risk profile.

[JAMIE]
Can we walk through those use cases in plain English?

[ALEX]
Sure. A read-only research setup is safest when you want analysis without modifications. Documentation or file generation adds writing capability. Full GitHub workflow combines repo-aware operations. Terminal access is powerful but should be used carefully. Conversational-only mode means no file access. Interactive wizard mode emphasizes guided Q and A.

[JAMIE]
So choosing tools is really choosing capability boundaries.

[ALEX]
Yes, and safety boundaries.

[JAMIE]
What about the body of the agent file?

[ALEX]
The body is the operational prompt. The template described here includes sections such as constraints, behavior, task name, output format, section header conventions, accessibility requirements, and scope boundaries. This is where you tell the agent what it should and should not do.

[JAMIE]
Give me a concrete example of why those sections matter.

[ALEX]
If you’re building an accessibility review agent, constraints might say “do not invent test results,” behavior might say “analyze semantic structure and keyboard implications,” output format might require headings and severity groupings, accessibility requirements might mandate navigable heading levels and descriptive link text, and scope boundaries might say “do not alter build configuration unless explicitly asked.”

[JAMIE]
So the structure disciplines the assistant.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And because this appendix is accessibility-focused, it explicitly includes accessibility requirements as part of the agent definition, not as an afterthought.

[JAMIE]
There’s also a learning-card section for .agent.md.

[ALEX]
Right, reinforcing that this file type is central enough to warrant recap and memorization.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How is .prompt.md different?

[ALEX]
A .prompt.md file defines a reusable prompt or slash command rather than a full agent persona. Think of it as a command-shaped task package.

[JAMIE]
So if an agent is “who you are,” a prompt is more like “what to do.”

[ALEX]
That’s a very good shorthand. The .prompt.md reference covers file locations, frontmatter, model fallback, tool priority when an agent is also specified, input parameters, body structure for referencing tools and files, an example accessibility update command, and behavior rules.

[JAMIE]
Input parameters sound especially useful.

[ALEX]
They are. They let a slash command accept values such as a file path, repository name, date range, or review target. That makes the command reusable without rewriting the prompt every time.

[JAMIE]
And tool priority when an agent is also specified?

[ALEX]
That’s about resolving authority. If a prompt calls an agent but also declares tools or expectations, the system needs a rule for which settings take precedence. The appendix makes clear that this interaction matters and should be designed intentionally.

[JAMIE]
And creating your own slash command follows the same general philosophy as creating an agent: name it well, scope it carefully, specify inputs, and define outputs.

[ALEX]
Yes, with the additional reminder that good slash commands reduce repetitive prompting and support consistent workflows.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now skills. Agent skills use SKILL.md and are described as a complete format reference too.

[JAMIE]
How should learners think about skills compared with agents and prompts?

[ALEX]
Skills are reusable capability modules. An agent is a persona plus behavior package. A prompt is a reusable command. A skill is a chunk of specialized know-how that can be loaded when needed.

[JAMIE]
And the appendix includes folder structure and file locations.

[ALEX]
Right. Skills live in a defined folder structure. Their frontmatter and body define what they do and how they should be invoked or loaded. There’s also a key concept called progressive loading.

[JAMIE]
What does that mean?

[ALEX]
VS Code may load skills progressively rather than all at once. In practical terms, that means relevant skills can become available when context suggests they’re needed, which helps manage scale and avoids overloading the model with every skill at all times.

[JAMIE]
That sounds like a performance and relevance strategy.

[ALEX]
It is. The appendix also notes slash command behavior for skills, which helps learners understand how skills may connect to command-driven workflows.

[JAMIE]
And there’s an example skill.

[ALEX]
Yes, an Accessibility Audit Skill. The example is organized with sections like when to use, procedure, and output format. That’s pedagogically important because it shows that even a skill should define activation conditions, repeatable steps, and a structured result.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Hooks are next, and I think some learners hear “hooks” and immediately worry.

[ALEX]
Fair reaction. Hooks are lifecycle automation defined in JSON. They can trigger at certain events and run commands. Powerful, but they need care.

[JAMIE]
What should learners remember?

[ALEX]
Locations, events, configuration format, command fields, and the input-output contract. Hooks respond to defined events, such as before a tool is used or after certain actions complete, depending on the supported hook system.

[JAMIE]
The appendix specifically mentions PreToolUse permission decisions.

[ALEX]
Yes. That means a hook can participate in deciding whether a tool use should be allowed. It’s part of the safety and governance story.

[JAMIE]
And exit codes?

[ALEX]
Exit codes communicate success, failure, or decision outcomes in automation flows. So if you’re debugging a hook or designing one, those codes matter.

[JAMIE]
This feels advanced, but still important for trustworthy workflows.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Even if a learner doesn’t write hooks immediately, they should know hooks exist as an automation and enforcement layer.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now a gentler file: preferences.md. This is presented as Accessibility Agents Personal Settings.

[JAMIE]
So this is less about repository policy and more about me.

[ALEX]
Correct. The full template includes fields like your GitHub username, repositories you work on most, preferred output format, notification priority, review comment tone, time zone, and accessibility context.

[JAMIE]
That accessibility context field is especially interesting.

[ALEX]
It is. It acknowledges that accessibility is not only an external product concern. It also affects how the assistant should communicate with you. Maybe you want concise heading-rich output, maybe minimal tables, maybe explicit keyboard steps, maybe strong text alternatives for visual descriptions.

[JAMIE]
And the appendix lists option sets for output format, notification priority, comment tone, and accessibility context.

[ALEX]
Yes. That helps standardize personalization while still allowing individual needs.

[JAMIE]
So a learner could effectively tell the system: I prefer structured prose over tables, I need higher priority alerts for accessibility regressions, I want review comments direct but respectful, and I’m in this time zone.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Troubleshooting time. What goes wrong most often?

[ALEX]
The appendix calls out a diagnostics area and common issues. First, viewing all loaded customizations. That’s important because many problems come down to “the file exists, but it isn’t being loaded.”

[JAMIE]
So visibility into loaded customizations is step one.

[ALEX]
Yes. Then common problems: the agent is not found when typing the at-name, instructions are not being applied, the instructions file is in the wrong place, or the slash command is not appearing.

[JAMIE]
And the likely root causes?

[ALEX]
Usually incorrect file location, unsupported naming, invalid frontmatter, discovery mismatch, or simply using a feature in a context where it isn’t supported. The reference strongly implies: check placement, naming, and product support matrix before assuming the model is broken.

[JAMIE]
That’s a very real lesson in tooling.

[ALEX]
Yes. Also, there’s a specific section on accessibility agents keyboard shortcuts. Even without reading each shortcut aloud here, the important point is that keyboard-first access matters, especially for blind and low-vision users. Learners should actively practice invoking chat, navigating heading-based output, opening accessible views, and moving through command interfaces without relying on the mouse.

[JAMIE]
So accessibility is present both in the content being analyzed and in the way we operate the tools.

[ALEX]
Absolutely.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The appendix also looks beyond custom files to smart actions, the browser agent, and third-party agents.

[JAMIE]
What’s the takeaway there?

[ALEX]
Smart Actions can complement accessibility workflows by offering contextual operations in supported environments. Browser Agent support matters for accessibility testing because many accessibility checks are inherently browser-centered: DOM behavior, keyboard interaction, live announcements, layout responsiveness, and rendered semantics. Third-party agents on GitHub.com or GitHub Cloud expand the ecosystem, but learners should evaluate capability, trust, and support carefully.

[JAMIE]
So the ecosystem is broader than just one editor feature.

[ALEX]
Yes, though the reference keeps VS Code and GitHub Copilot at the center for practical day-to-day customization.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap up, can we do a compact decision guide? If I need to customize behavior, how do I choose the right primitive?

[ALEX]
Absolutely.
If you want broad, always-on project guidance, use .github/copilot-instructions.md.
If you want tool-agnostic or monorepo guidance, consider AGENTS.md, with caution around nested behavior.
If you want Claude Code compatibility, use CLAUDE.md where appropriate.
If you want rules only for certain files, use .instructions.md with applyTo globs.
If you want a named assistant persona with defined tools and behavior, create a .agent.md file.
If you want a reusable slash command, create a .prompt.md file.
If you want reusable specialized know-how, define a skill with SKILL.md.
If you want lifecycle automation or policy enforcement, use hooks JSON.
If you want your own personal defaults and communication preferences, use preferences.md.

[JAMIE]
That is the map.

[ALEX]
And if you’re unsure, start simple. Don’t build an agent, a prompt, a skill, and a hook on day one. Begin with always-on instructions and one targeted instruction file. Then add a custom agent or slash command once you know what repetition you’re trying to eliminate.

[JAMIE]
That advice probably saves people a lot of confusion.

[ALEX]
Usually, yes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Any final note on sources and trustworthiness?

[ALEX]
Yes. The appendix points learners back to authoritative documentation: GitHub Docs, Copilot docs, support matrices for custom instructions, documentation about custom agents, and the changelog. That matters because these features are evolving. File names, precedence rules, and platform support can shift. So the best habit is to keep a stable mental model, but verify current behavior against official docs.

[JAMIE]
And maybe the most important accessibility takeaway is that output structure is part of quality, not decoration.

[ALEX]
Beautifully said. Headings, navigable sections, explicit scope, clear constraints, and predictable formatting help everyone, and they are especially valuable for blind and low-vision contributors.

[JAMIE]
So the real skill here is not just learning a bunch of filenames. It’s learning how to design trustworthy, reusable, accessible collaboration with AI tools.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And once that clicks, these files stop feeling like clutter and start feeling like a well-organized toolkit.

# Appendix L: Accessibility Agents Reference
>
> **Listen to Episode 39:** [Accessibility Agents - Complete Reference](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 19: Accessibility Agents](19-accessibility-agents.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 20](20-build-your-agent.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: MCP overview](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/building-copilot-extensions/about-building-copilot-extensions) | [VS Code: Custom Agents](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/custom-agents)
>
> **Note:** The "Building Copilot Extensions" docs now redirect to MCP documentation. The GitHub App-based Copilot Extensions model has been superseded by MCP servers as the standard extensibility mechanism. Custom `.agent.md` files remain the primary agent persona format.

## Complete Reference - Agents, Slash Commands, Instructions, Configuration Levels, and All File Formats

> This is your comprehensive reference for Accessibility Agents and the full VS Code Copilot customization system. The ecosystem includes **80 agents** across **3 teams** and **5 platforms**, plus 54+ slash commands, 25+ reusable skills, and 6 instruction files. For the lesson, see [Chapter 19: Accessibility Agents](19-accessibility-agents.md). For Copilot keyboard shortcuts and Chat features, see [Appendix K: GitHub Copilot Reference](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md).

## Table of Contents

1. [The Full Agent Ecosystem](#1-the-full-agent-ecosystem)
2. [GitHub Workflow Agents - Quick Reference](#2-github-workflow-agents---quick-reference)
3. [Slash Commands and Prompts](#3-slash-commands-and-prompts)
4. [Customization Primitives - Decision Guide](#4-customization-primitives---decision-guide)
5. [Scope and Priority - All Levels](#5-scope-and-priority---all-levels)
6. [Always-On Instructions - All File Types](#6-always-on-instructions---all-file-types)
7. [File-Based Instructions (.instructions.md)](#7-file-based-instructions-instructionsmd)
8. [.agent.md - Complete Format Reference](#8-agentmd---complete-format-reference)
9. [.prompt.md - Complete Format Reference](#9-promptmd---complete-format-reference)
10. [Agent Skills (SKILL.md) - Complete Format Reference](#10-agent-skills-skillmd---complete-format-reference)
11. [Hooks (.json) - Lifecycle Automation](#11-hooks-json---lifecycle-automation)
12. [preferences.md - Accessibility Agents Personal Settings](#12-preferencesmd---accessibility-agents-personal-settings)
13. [Diagnostics and Troubleshooting](#13-diagnostics-and-troubleshooting)
14. [Smart Actions, Browser Agent, and Third-Party Agents](#14-smart-actions-browser-agent-and-third-party-agents)
15. [Further Reading](#15-further-reading)

## 1. The Full Agent Ecosystem

Accessibility Agents includes 80 agents organized into three specialized teams, available on five platforms. All agents run on GitHub Copilot in VS Code; many also run on Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, and Codex CLI via platform-specific installation paths.

### Platforms

| Platform | Agent Format | When to Use | Features |
| ----------  | -------------  | ----------  | --------- |
| **GitHub Copilot** (VS Code) | `.github/agents/*.agent.md` | Daily workflow in the editor | Full tool access, inline suggestions, Accessible View |
| **Claude Code** | Per-agent definitions + hook enforcement | Autonomous multi-file tasks | Full code generation, terminal control, file management |
| **Gemini CLI** | Skills-based agents with Gemini extension | Command-line workflows | Fast iteration, built-in Google Search integration |
| **Claude Desktop** | MCP server integration | Desktop app for extended sessions | Persistent context, project continuity, long-running tasks |
| **Codex CLI** | Codex-specific agent definitions | Experimental workflows | 11 specialized roles, TOML-based configuration |

### Team 1: Accessibility (40 agents)

This team audits and remediates web and document accessibility across all WCAG criteria, from basic to AAA conformance. Includes specialized agents for native mobile apps, email accessibility, media, data visualization, design systems, and cognitive accessibility.

| Agent | Type | What It Does |
| -------  | ------  | -------------  |
| `@accessibility-lead` | Orchestrator | Delegates multi-agent accessibility audits to specialist agents |

## 5. Scope and Priority - All Levels

Every customization file exists at one of three scopes. VS Code combines all matching files from all scopes and sends them to the model.

### The Three Scopes

| Scope | Where Files Live | Who Shares It |
| -------  | -----------------  | ---------------  |
| **User / Personal** | VS Code profile folder | You only - follows Settings Sync across devices |
| **Workspace** | `.github/` and related folders in the repo | Everyone who clones the repo |
| **Organization** | GitHub organization settings (Enterprise/Team) | Everyone in the org |

### Priority Order (highest wins in conflicts)

1. **Personal / User-level** - your profile instructions override everything
2. **Workspace / Repository-level** - `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.github/agents/*.agent.md`
3. **Organization-level** - organization-defined custom instructions (lowest priority)

### User-Level File Locations (Personal, Cross-Workspace)

All of these files roam with your VS Code Settings Sync.

| File Type | Location on Windows | Location on macOS/Linux |
| -----------  | ---------------------  | ------------------------  |
| Instructions | `%APPDATA%\Code - Insiders\User\prompts\*.instructions.md` | `~/Library/Application Support/Code - Insiders/User/prompts/` |

## 7. File-Based Instructions (`.instructions.md`)

File-based instructions load conditionally - either when the files you are editing match a glob pattern, or when the agent determines the instruction is relevant to the current task.

**Use for:** Language-specific rules, framework conventions, module-specific standards that only apply to part of the codebase.

### File Locations

| Scope | Location |
| -------  | ----------  |
| Workspace | `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` |
| Additional workspace folders | Configure with `chat.instructionsFilesLocations` setting |
| User / Personal | VS Code profile prompts folder (`*.instructions.md`) |

### Frontmatter Fields

```yaml
name: "Display Name"           # Optional - defaults to filename; shown in UI
description: "Use when..."     # Optional - enables on-demand discovery; be keyword-rich
applyTo: "**/*.py"             # Optional - glob pattern(s) for automatic application
```

### The `applyTo` Glob Pattern

`applyTo` specifies which files trigger automatic inclusion of these instructions. When a file matching the pattern is part of the chat context, the instructions are included automatically.

```yaml
applyTo: "**"                          # ALWAYS included (use carefully - applies everywhere)
applyTo: "**/*.py"                     # All Python files
applyTo: "**/*.{ts,tsx}"               # TypeScript and TSX files
applyTo: "docs/**"                     # Everything under docs/
applyTo: ["src/**", "lib/**"]          # Multiple patterns (OR - either match triggers inclusion)
applyTo: src/**, lib/**                # Same without array syntax
applyTo: "**/*.test.{js,ts}"          # Only test files
applyTo: ".github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/**"  # Only issue template files
```

**If `applyTo` is omitted:** The instruction is NOT applied automatically. It can still be added manually via the Chat context menu, or picked up by the agent if the `description` semantically matches the current task.

### Discovery Modes

| Mode | Trigger | When to Use |
| ------  | ---------  | -------------  |
| **Automatic** (`applyTo` set) | When matching files are in the chat context | Language rules, framework patterns, folder-specific standards |
| **On-demand** (`description` set, no `applyTo`) | Agent detects task relevance from description keywords | Migration guides, refactoring rules, API design patterns |
| **Manual** | User selects "Add Context → Instructions" in Chat | Ad-hoc attachment for one-off situations |

### Example: Accessibility-Specific Instructions

```markdown
name: "Accessible Markdown Standards"
description: "Use when writing, editing, or reviewing Markdown documentation. Covers heading hierarchy, link text, alt text, and table structure."
applyTo: "**/*.md"

# Markdown Accessibility Standards

- Never skip heading levels (H1 → H2 → H3; H1 → H3 is a WCAG 1.3.1 violation)
- Use descriptive link text: never "click here", "read more", or bare URLs
- Every informational image must have alt text describing what it conveys
- Every decorative image must use empty alt: `![](image.png)` or `alt=""`
- Tables must have header rows using `|---|` Markdown syntax
- Ordered lists (`1.`) only for genuinely sequential steps; use unordered (`-`) otherwise
```

### Example: YAML Issue Template Instructions

```markdown
name: "Issue Template YAML"
description: "Use when writing or reviewing GitHub issue templates in YAML format"
applyTo: ".github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/**/*.{yml,yaml}"

# Issue Template YAML Standards

- Every field must have a non-empty `label`
- Dropdowns must list at least 2 options
- Use `required: true` only for fields that truly block triage without them
- Prefer `textarea` for free-form text; use `input` only for short identifiers
- Every template must have a `name`, `description`, and `title` prefix
```

#### Command Palette method

### Writing Effective Instructions

Guidance from GitHub's accessibility team on writing instructions that Copilot actually follows:

**Do:**

- **Use normative language.** Write `MUST`, `MUST NOT`, `SHOULD`, `SHOULD NOT`, and `MAY` for rules. LLMs respond well to these terms because they reduce ambiguity -- the same words used in WCAG. Example: `Keyboard shortcuts MUST NOT override browser or OS shortcuts.`
- **Use lists and checklists.** Structured lists provide guardrails that keep Copilot on track. Format accessibility requirements as a checklist so no criterion is overlooked.
- **Specify your versions and standards.** `This application MUST conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA` is more useful than a general reference to accessibility. Include your design system's component names and flag deprecated components explicitly: `DeprecatedButton MUST NOT be used; use NewAccessibleButton instead.`
- **Focus on what Copilot doesn't already know.** Instructions should add net-new information -- your team's conventions, exceptions, and priorities -- not restate what Copilot was trained on.
- **Keep instructions concise.** Overly long instructions reduce model performance. Summarize the most important rules rather than listing every possible case.

**Don't:**

- **Don't paste full guidelines.** Copilot is already trained on WCAG, ARIA, and HTML standards. Copying large sections of a spec into instructions wastes context and rarely improves output. Focus on your team's specific deviations and priorities instead.
- **Don't reference external links.** By design, Copilot does not fetch URLs in custom instructions (a deliberate privacy and security protection). A link is useful as a human reference but has no effect on Copilot's behavior. Write the relevant rules directly into the instructions text.
- **Don't reference private repositories.** Copilot cannot access private repo content from within another repository's instructions. Write the guidance inline.
- **Use role-based prompting carefully.** Assigning a persona (`You are the lead accessibility expert...`) can be effective, but any persona can carry assumptions from training data. If you use role prompting, be specific about skills and responsibilities, stay neutral, and use professional functional language.

**Share your instructions:** The [github/awesome-copilot](https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot) repository collects community-contributed instructions files. Before submitting, review your file to confirm it contains no sensitive or confidential information.

```yaml

description: "Use when..."           # Required - keyword-rich trigger phrases for on-demand discovery
argument-hint: "Optional input..."   # Optional - hint shown when skill is selected as slash command

### Slash Command Behavior

| `user-invocable` | `disable-model-invocation` | Result |
| ------------------  | --------------------------  | --------  |
| true (default) | false (default) | Appears as `/command` AND auto-loads |
| false | false | Does NOT appear as `/command`; auto-loads only |
| true | true | Appears as `/command`; does NOT auto-load |
| false | true | Neither `/command` nor auto-load |

### Progressive Loading - How VS Code Loads Skills

1. **Discovery (~100 tokens):** Reads `name` and `description` to decide if the skill is relevant
2. **Instructions (<5000 tokens):** Loads the full `SKILL.md` body when the skill is relevant
3. **Resources:** Additional files (`scripts/`, `references/`) only load when explicitly referenced from `SKILL.md`

**Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines.** Move reference material to `references/` folder files.

description: "Audit Markdown files for accessibility violations. Use for heading hierarchy, link text quality, alt text, and WCAG compliance checks."

- When asked to check accessibility compliance of docs
- After generating new documentation content
- During content review for WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.4, 1.1.1

1. Run the audit script: [audit.sh](./scripts/audit.sh)
2. Review output for heading hierarchy violations (H1→H3 skips)

4. Verify alt text on all images

- Medium risk: degraded accessibility
- Low risk: improvement opportunities
- Include WCAG criterion for each finding
```

## 11. Hooks (`.json`) - Lifecycle Automation

Hooks execute shell commands at specific points in an agent's lifecycle. They are deterministic - they run regardless of what the agent was prompted to do.

**Use hooks for enforcement, not guidance.** For behavior you want to enforce - blocking commands, auto-running formatters, requiring approval - use hooks. For behavior you want to encourage - coding standards, tone, output format - use instructions.

### File Locations

| Scope | Location | Committed? |
| -------  | ----------  | -----------  |
| Workspace (team-shared) | `.github/hooks/*.json` | Yes |
| Workspace (local) | `.claude/settings.local.json` | No (gitignored) |
| Workspace | `.claude/settings.json` | Yes |
| User / Personal | `~/.claude/settings.json` | Personal only |

Hooks from all locations are combined - workspace and user hooks do not override each other.

### Hook Events

| Event | When It Fires |
| -------  | --------------  |
| `SessionStart` | First prompt of a new agent session |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | User submits any prompt |
| `PreToolUse` | Immediately before any tool is invoked |
| `PostToolUse` | After successful tool invocation |
| `PreCompact` | Before context compaction |
| `SubagentStart` | When a subagent begins |
| `SubagentStop` | When a subagent ends |
| `Stop` | When the agent session ends |

### Configuration Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": ".github/hooks/validate-before-edit.sh",
        "timeout": 15
      }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "npx prettier --write",
        "windows": "npx.cmd prettier --write",
        "timeout": 30
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Hook Command Fields

| Field | Required | Description |
| -------  | ----------  | -------------  |
| `type` | Yes | Must be `"command"` |
| `command` | Yes | Shell command to run (default for all platforms) |
| `windows` | No | Windows-specific override |
| `linux` | No | Linux-specific override |
| `osx` | No | macOS-specific override |
| `cwd` | No | Working directory for the command |
| `env` | No | Environment variable overrides |
| `timeout` | No | Max seconds before killing the process |

### Input/Output Contract

Hooks receive JSON on `stdin`. They can return JSON on `stdout`:

```json
{
  "continue": true,
  "stopReason": "optional message if blocking",
  "systemMessage": "optional context injected into the agent session"
}
```

#### `PreToolUse` permission decisions

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
    "permissionDecision": "allow",
    "permissionDecisionReason": "Safe read-only operation"
  }
}
```

Permission decisions: `"allow"` | `"ask"` (prompt user) | `"deny"` (block the tool call)

#### Exit codes

- `0` - success; agent continues
- `2` - blocking error; agent stops
- Other - non-blocking warning

### Learning Cards: Hooks

**Screen reader users:**

- Hooks are JSON files, not Markdown -- navigate them in the editor with arrow keys; each hook event (e.g., `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`) is a key in the `"hooks"` object
- Hook output is returned as JSON on `stdout` -- the `"continue"` field (true/false) determines whether the agent proceeds; listen for the `"stopReason"` message if the hook blocks an action
- The `"permissionDecision"` values (`allow`, `ask`, `deny`) control tool access -- `ask` triggers a confirmation dialog that your screen reader will announce as a standard VS Code dialog

**Low-vision users:**

- JSON syntax requires careful attention to braces, brackets, and commas -- use VS Code's bracket pair colorization (`editor.bracketPairColorization.enabled`) and increase font size to verify structure
- The hook events table maps each event name to when it fires -- zoom in on the "When It Fires" column to understand the lifecycle timing
- Hook errors appear in the agent session output -- look for non-zero exit codes or `"continue": false` in the output pane

**Sighted users:**

- The hook events table lists 8 lifecycle events -- `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` are the most commonly used for validation and formatting enforcement
- The configuration format example shows the JSON structure with `command`, `timeout`, and platform-specific overrides -- copy this template and modify the command paths for your project
- Hooks from workspace (`.github/hooks/`) and user (`~/.claude/settings.json`) locations are combined, not overridden -- check both locations if a hook is firing unexpectedly

## 13. Diagnostics and Troubleshooting

### View All Loaded Customizations

To see every instruction file, agent, prompt, and skill currently loaded and any errors:

1. In Copilot Chat, select the gear icon (Configure Chat) → **Diagnostics**
2. Or right-click in the Chat view → **Diagnostics**

This shows: which files were found, which were loaded, which have errors, and from which scope (user vs workspace vs organization).

### Common Issues

#### Agent not found when typing `@agent-name`

1. Verify `.github/agents/[name].agent.md` exists in your open workspace folder
2. Check that the YAML frontmatter has no syntax errors (missing quotes, wrong indentation)
3. `Ctrl+Shift+P` → "Reload Window"
4. Check that the `name` field in the frontmatter matches what you are typing

#### Instructions not being applied

1. For `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: file must be at workspace root in the `.github/` folder
2. For `*.instructions.md`: check that `applyTo` glob matches the file you are editing, and that `chat.includeApplyingInstructions` is `true` in VS Code settings
3. For `AGENTS.md`: check that `chat.useAgentsMdFile` is `true`
4. Use Diagnostics view (above) to verify the file was found and loaded

#### Instructions file in wrong place

- Add custom locations: `chat.instructionsFilesLocations` setting accepts an array of additional folder paths

#### Slash command not appearing

1. Verify `.github/prompts/[name].prompt.md` exists
2. `Ctrl+Shift+P` → "Reload Window"
3. File must use `.prompt.md` extension (not just `.md`)

## 14. Smart Actions, Browser Agent, and Third-Party Agents

### Smart Actions and Accessibility Agents

VS Code 1.120+ introduces **Smart Actions** (automated suggestions for commit messages, symbol renaming, error fixing, and semantic search). These complement Accessibility Agents by automating routine tasks that don't require conversational reasoning.

**Workflow:** Use Smart Actions (`Ctrl+.`) for quick fixes and accessibility agents (`` `@accessibility-lead` ``, `` `@wcag-guide` ``) for audits, explanations, and strategic guidance.

| Use Smart Actions For | Use Accessibility Agents For |
|----------------------|------------------------------|
| Generate commit messages | Plan complex refactoring |
| Rename variables consistently | Full WCAG 2.2 audits |
| Fix linting errors | Custom accessibility rules |
| Find related code quickly | Detailed remediation guidance |
| Repair broken imports | Document compliance mapping |

See [Appendix K: Smart Actions](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md#4c-smart-actions) for keyboard shortcuts and accessibility workflows.

### Browser Agent and Accessibility Testing

The **Browser Agent (Experimental)** can open and test web applications, but it requires human verification for accessibility claims. Pair Browser Agent with manual screen reader testing and structured Accessibility Agents audits.

**Best practice workflow:**

1. Use Browser Agent to take screenshots and verify layout (quick visual check)
2. Use `` `@web-accessibility-wizard` `` to run structured audit (axe-core, semantic analysis)
3. Do manual screen reader + keyboard testing to verify agent findings
4. Use Accessibility Agents for remediation guidance and compliance mapping

See [Appendix K: Browser Agent (Experimental)](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md#4d-browser-agent-experimental) and [Chapter 15: Code Review](15-code-review.md) for testing best practices.

### Third-Party Agents on GitHub.com and GitHub Cloud

GitHub supports assigning cloud agents to issues and pull requests. You can use Copilot Agent, Claude (by Anthropic), or OpenAI Codex for task automation at scale.

**Accessibility workflow for cloud agents:**

- Tag issues with labels that trigger agent assignments (`` `agent-review`, `documentation` ``)
- Create a custom instruction or hook that directs agents to consider accessibility
- Review agent PRs with Accessibility Agents before merging
- Use `` `@compliance-mapping` `` to verify WCAG alignment of agent-generated code

**GitHub cloud agent assignment syntax:**

```
@copilot please implement this feature with accessibility best practices in mind.
Reference: [Appendix K: GitHub Agentic Workflows](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md#14-github-agentic-workflows-and-third-party-agents)
```

For detailed information about cloud agents, third-party integrations, and platform-specific deployment, see [Appendix K: GitHub Agentic Workflows and Third-Party Agents](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md#14-github-agentic-workflows-and-third-party-agents).
